TL;DR
HDD - older, cheaper, higher capacity, much slower
SSD - newer, expensive, lower capacity, Much Much Faster Put Operating System on a SSD, and the rest of your files on a HDD

~

There are two main types of hard drives. There is a hard drive disk (aka hdd, the traditional type) and a solid state drive (aka ssd, the newer type).

~

I'll start of with how they operate.

A hdd has spinning disks similar to a cd, dvd, blu ray, etc. The disks store the data in a similar fashion as well. The moving disks is what makes them fragile

A ssd dose not have moving internals. It relies on microchips instead of disks. This is more like a flash or thumb drive. They are much more durable because nothing moves inside.

~

Moving on to pros and cons of each.

HDD- Older technology, but still progressing and great. Much cheaper than ssd. Comes in much larger storage sizes, ie 750GB, 2TB (or ~2000GB). You will see these usually range from 250GB to 3TB (~3000GB). You can get them smaller though. Older ones can be very small. Usually gives some warnings before it fails completely.

SSD- Newer technology. Definitely more expensive, but are getting cheaper every year. Smaller size, but you can find them around 1TB (with a very hefty price tag). Typically last much longer and can take much more of a beating than a hdd. PC enthusiasts use them is because they are faster... A lot faster. They tend to fail suddenly with little to no warning though.

A hdd speed is limited by how fast it can move it's internals, where a ssd has no moving parts. A ssd is limited on how fast it can send an electronic current. A faster hard drive will result in transferring data faster, such as uploading, downloading, or copying files. This means things will start faster, save faster, load faster, ect. Anything that involves data will be faster.

~

I'll now explain how people use them.

People often use both a ssd and a hdd to reduce costs and increase storage capacity. It's very common for people to install the Operating System (Windows 7 for example) on the ssd and put nearly everything else on the ssd. 120gb ssd will be big enough if you only want to put your OS and a couple other things (like Microsoft Office) on it. If you want to store a couple games as well, you should go with 200GB+. All your other games, pictures, downloads will go onto your hdd.

The reason people do this is because your Operating System is always running. This reduces the strain on you primary hard drive (the hdd) and allows it to focus only on whatever programs you are running. This drastically speeds up the computer's read and write time (aka transferring data stuff). This also gives you some benefit of the reliability of a ssd. Because the ssd has the operating system on it, the operating system is (mostly) safe from failure. However, your storage files are not. This means if your hdd fails, you slap in a new one and start all over (files are lost, but you don't have to reinstall your OS).

~

Low-Mid range computers- HDD only
Mid-High range computers- SSD/HDD combo
High-Ridiculous computers- SSD/HDD combo or only SSD (very expensive)

~

HDD- Older technology, but still progressing and great. Much cheaper than ssd. Comes in much larger storage sizes, ie 750GB, 2TB (or ~2000GB). You will see these usually range from 250GB to 3TB (~3000GB).

8 TB drives are easily available and 10TB drives are being produced in small numbers.

A hdd speed is limited by how fast it can move it's internals, where a ssd has no moving parts. A ssd is limited on how fast it can send an electronic current. A faster hard drive will result in transferring data faster, such as uploading, downloading, or copying files. This means things will start faster, save faster, load faster, ect. Anything that involves data will be faster.

Don't forget bus speed, an SSD on a SATA2 link is just as slow as a HDD for sequential access.

There is also a third option, the SSHD. A hybrid of the two where both drives are combined into one and software directs their joint function (which is why some people are create a similar setup with separate SSDs and HDDs). The hybrid drive places frequently referenced data on the SSD portion of the driver for faster retrieval and the HDD does the bulk of standard storage. Think along the lines of a cache. However, there is a bit of a 'break in' period where the drive must determine what to place on the SSD before the benefits can be fully realized.

There are notable performance increases over a standard HDD; however, it is not quite as good as an SSD in terms of read and write times. Being a happy medium between the two, the price matches. An equivalent SSD is more than an equivalent SSHD is more than an equivalent HDD.
